title: Anatomy of a JWT: decode one by hand

cards.s: Anatomy of a JWT: decode one by hand
cards.html: A JWT (JSON Web Token, pronounced "jot", defined in RFC 7519) is three base64url strings joined by dots: header.payload.signature. The header says how it was signed, the payload says who and what, and the signature proves both are genuine.

eyJ0eXAiOiJKV1QiLCJhbGciOiJSUzI1NiIsImtpZCI6IjIwMjYtMTEifQ   ← header
.
eyJpc3MiOiJodHRwczovL2xhcmF2ZWwuZXhhbXBsZS50ZXN0IiwiYXVkIjoi...  ← payload (shortened)
.
kQ3vX9...(342 characters for a 2048-bit RSA key)...              ← signature

A handy tell: every JWT starts with eyJ. That's what {" looks like in base64. If you see eyJ in a log line, someone logged a token.

The header above is copied from the real ai_token examples in the app guides. The payload is an illustrative one built for this guide: the claim names and shapes match the AI guide exactly, but the issuer https://laravel.example.test, the user and the times are made up.

Decoded:

{"typ": "JWT", "alg": "RS256", "kid": "2026-11"}
FieldMeaningOur valueWhat you do with it
algAlgorithm used for the signatureAlways RS256Refuse anything else. Never let this field pick the algorithm (next section).
typMedia type of the tokenJWTInformational; not a security check.
kidKey id: which of the issuer's keys signed ite.g. 2026-11Look up the matching public key in the issuer's JWKS.

The header is not trusted when you first read it. An attacker writes whatever they like in it. You read it only to decide which key to try, then the signature check tells you whether to believe any of it.

A claim is one statement the issuer makes about the subject, as a JSON key and value. "role is student" is a claim. Decoded, our illustrative user token reads:

{
  "iss": "https://laravel.example.test",
  "aud": "ai-api",
  "sub": "141",
  "role": "student",
  "scope": "face:verify id:verify ocr:submit image:check",
  "inst": 12,
  "iat": 1795341600,
  "nbf": 1795341600,
  "exp": 1795342500,
  "jti": "3b8f0c52-7a1e-4d2b-9c4f-6e1a2d3b4c5d",
  "ver": 1
}
1795341600 is a Unix timestamp: seconds since 1 January 1970, 00:00 UTC. It is 2026-11-22 10:00:00 UTC. exp is exactly 900 seconds later, 10:15:00, which matches the 15-minute user-token lifetime.

Claims come in two kinds. Registered claims are the short names RFC 7519 defines so every library understands them. Private claims are names an issuer and its consumers agree on between themselves. Here is every claim we use:

ClaimKindTypeMeaning (from the AI guide)Your check
issRegistered (issuer)stringWhich Laravel environment issued it: https://<laravel-host>, no trailing slashMust be in your trusted-issuer list and match exactly
audRegistered (audience)stringAlways ai-apiMust equal ai-api
subRegistered (subject)stringUser id, or laravel for the service tokenMust be present
iatRegistered (issued at)integer, Unix secondsWhen it was issuedMust be present; useful in logs
nbfRegistered (not before)integer, Unix secondsValid fromMust not be in the future (30 s leeway)
expRegistered (expiration)integer, Unix secondsExpires atMust be in the future (30 s leeway)
jtiRegistered (JWT id)string (UUID)Unique token id, for logsLog it; no check needed
rolePrivatestringstudent, registrant, faculty, admin or serviceMust be present

ClaimKindTypeMeaning (from the AI guide)Your check
scopePrivatestringSpace-separated permissions, e.g. face:verify id:verifyMust be present; endpoint's scope must be in it, else 403
instPrivateintegerUniversity id. Not in the service token.Pass to the endpoint for logging and per-university limits
verPrivateintegerReserved for a future revoke check. Not in the service token.Ignore it for now
exam_idPrivateintegerOptional. Not sent yet.Ignore

A few details worth noticing:

  • sub is a string, even for a numeric user id. RFC 7519 says sub is a string. Don't compare it to an integer.
  • aud can legally be a string or an array in the RFC. Ours is a string, and PyJWT handles both when you pass audience="ai-api".
  • scope is a single space-separated string, the convention from OAuth 2.0 (RFC 6749 and RFC 8693). It is not a JSON array. Split on spaces.
  • The "draft, please confirm" label. The scopes-per-role table in the AI guide is marked as a draft. Treat scope strings as configuration you might need to change, not constants scattered through code.

cards.s: The service token looks like this
cards.html:
Same shape, fewer claims, shorter life. An illustrative decode:

{
  "iss": "https://laravel.example.test",
  "aud": "ai-api",
  "sub": "laravel",
  "role": "service",
  "scope": "<every scope>",
  "iat": 1795341600,
  "nbf": 1795341600,
  "exp": 1795341900,
  "jti": "9a1d2e3f-..."
}

No inst and no ver, sub is the literal string laravel, and exp - iat is 300 seconds (5 minutes). The guide says the service role "has every scope"; the exact string is whatever Laravel puts there, so your code should just check membership like any other token.

The third part is the base64url-encoded RSA signature over the exact bytes header_b64 + "." + payload_b64. Not over the decoded JSON. That matters: if anything re-encodes the JSON (different key order, different spacing), the signature no longer matches. You never rebuild a token; you verify the string you received.

cards.s: Decode it yourself in four lines
cards.html:
import base64, json

def b64url_decode(part: str) -> bytes:
    return base64.urlsafe_b64decode(part + "=" * (-len(part) % 4))

header_b64, payload_b64, signature_b64 = token.split(".")
print(json.loads(b64url_decode(header_b64)))
print(json.loads(b64url_decode(payload_b64)))

Or with the library (we'll use these two calls in the middleware, and only for choosing the key):

import jwt  # PyJWT

jwt.get_unverified_header(token)                                  # {'typ': 'JWT', 'alg': 'RS256', 'kid': '2026-11'}
jwt.decode(token, options={"verify_signature": False})["iss"]     # 'https://laravel.example.test'

cards.s: Decode it yourself in four lines
cards.html: The word unverified is a warning label, not a technicality. What these calls return could have been typed by an attacker. You may use it to choose which key to verify with, because a wrong choice just leads to a failed verification. You must not use it to decide anything else.

cards.s: Why the apps must not decode the token
cards.html: The app guides tell React and mobile to "treat ai_token as an opaque string. Don't decode it; use ai_token_expires_in for timing." An opaque token is one the holder treats as a meaningless blob. This lets Laravel and the AI team change the claims later without breaking any app. The AI service is the token's audience, so it's the only party that reads the claims, and only after verifying.

quiz.q: How many dot-separated parts does a signed JWT have?

quiz.why: Reject tokens after exp (allowing small clock skew).

quiz.q: Why should client apps treat the token as opaque?
o: Only the verifying service should rely on its contents; the format may change

quiz.q: Decoding a JWT without verifying the signature is fine for access decisions.
quiz.why: Myth. Unverified claims can be forged; verify first.
